sections.topic_sentence: Agentic software engineering is a fast-evolving topic, and it seems that many concepts have been given overlapping or contradictory names.
The ideas the whole argument turns on — the two theses, the conversion that grows the environment, the governing metaphor, and the vocabulary of models underneath them.
What a fleet of coding agents is, and the ways it comes apart.
The environment that holds the fleet to a standard, and the mechanisms it is built from.
Scaling a fleet hits a wall, the way scaling a team does — but a different one.

sections.topic_sentence: Engineering ran on the same handful of activities long before software, and software inherits them whole: **requirements**, **specification**, **design**, **implementation** (for software, writing the code), **validation**, and **maintenance**.

Process models reorder the activities, never replace them.

sections.topic_sentence: Modern agent architectures already externalize knowledge.

points.text: Agent architectures already externalize knowledge; a knowledge graph serves as an external reasoning substrate.
MAGE begins from the same observation, then asks how knowledge should be represented so the environment, not only the agent, can reason over it.

sections.heading_text: Derive and join; do not repeat
sections.topic_sentence: A model here is **derived** — from the code, or the code from it — never kept beside the code as a parallel document.

sections.topic_sentence: The purest model-from-code artifact is the repository graph a growing class of tools now hands a coding agent: a parser walks the repository into a persistent, queryable graph of its entities and relations — functions, classes, imports, calls, endpoints, schemas, tables — so the agent reasons through the graph instead of re-reading raw files.

points.text: A code graph recovers structure; an authored model declares intent.

sections.heading_text: Who owns each piece, and what may cross a boundary
sections.topic_sentence: The next question is the one an agent asks before it edits a line: *where am I, and what may this file touch?* The **component and zone model** answers it — a typed catalog that gives every component a code zone (its focus directories, its tags, its boundary kind, the external seams it may cross).

points.text: Descriptive facts are derivable; intent-bearing facts are authored.

sections.heading_text: What must hold across every interleaving
sections.topic_sentence: *What runs at once, and what stays true across every schedule?* Concurrency is where a correct-in-isolation design becomes a source of races, deadlocks, and torn writes, and the answer cannot be a thought experiment about interleavings.

points.text: The synchronization model declares every lock and its required ordering.

sections.heading_text: Two ways to make a concurrent write safe
sections.topic_sentence: Above the raw locks sit two registries that draw a distinction worth naming, because confusing them is how a corruption bug hides inside a load limit.

points.text: Capping how-many and allowing exactly-one fail differently.

sections.topic_sentence: All three concurrency models hang their invariant tables on one shared method, and it is trunk machinery rather than a model of the running system.

points.text: An invariant's temporal form routes its exhaustive checker, so a mis-declared shape is a build failure.

sections.topic_sentence: *Where does each part run, and which of those placements is a correctness decision?* A functionally correct system can still be mis-deployed.

points.text: The deployment-topology model declares where each service runs, and parity holds it to reality.

sections.heading_text: Correctness in the graph, resource limits in a profile
sections.topic_sentence: The placement models raise one more question — *what resources constrain execution?* — and answering it well turns on a single modeling principle, the most portable idea in this chapter: **correctness dependencies stay in the graph; host-specific resource limits live in a scheduler profile.**

points.text: Correctness dependencies stay in the graph; host-specific resource limits live in a scheduler profile.

sections.topic_sentence: That policy models the *load-and-cost* half of execution.

points.text: Model only where a failure lives; the pure-latency slice stayed empty until an incident filled it.

sections.topic_sentence: One last behavioral question an agent asks before it changes the ground everything runs on: *which mechanisms assume the substrate I am about to replace?* The **substrate-dependency model** makes each governance mechanism declare, as typed metadata, the substrate assumption it bakes in — bound to one substrate, substrate-aware, or substrate-agnostic.

points.text: Declared substrate stances make a migration blast radius computable.

sections.heading_text: The Scenarios View: what the system does for someone

points.text: Projecting coverage onto nodes makes an untested invariant visible.

sections.heading_text:
Example — Spotify
Migration at fleet scale stays incremental: you target a change, schedule it across the estate,
drain it, and keep a human on the exceptions. Spotify is the evidence it holds at organizational
size — a fleet-wide migration that once drew in hundreds of teams and ran for weeks is now scoped
by one engineer over a few days, the tooling targeting and scheduling the work while agents
implement it concurrently and the engineer watches the fleet and handles the exceptions rather
than typing each change [cite:spotify2026honk]. What to imitate is the placement, not the tool:
put the scarce human decision upstream — *what, where, when, whether* — and let the environment
carry the change onward, the same move the strategies above run at a single-subsystem grain. The
takeaway is that scale does not undo the incremental discipline; it raises the payoff, so the move
that repays weeks on one subsystem repays far more across a fleet.
